BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r1.claim: Al-Harali maps al-Fatiha's verses to the seven letters: praise, lawful and forbidden, command and prohibition, clear and ambiguous, then the corresponding petitions; its opening gathers all seven.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r1.anchor: فالآية الأولى تشتمل على حرف الحمد السابع

BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r2.claim: He offers two readings of the merciful names: universal mercy permits created benefits while specific mercy protects from harm; he says the nearer reading is general lordly beneficence and a special divine mercy directed to felicity.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r2.anchor: وأما الرحيمية فطهرتهم من مضار أبدانهم ورجاسة نفوسهم ومجهلة قلوبهم

BURSEVI:v1p2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2/r1.claim: The surah is Fatiha because it opens the codex, instruction, Qur'an recitation, prayer, speech, revelation, the aims of this life, and the gates of Paradise.
BURSEVI:v1p2/r1.anchor: لافتتاح المصاحف والتعليم وقراءة القرآن والصلاة بها وإما لأن الحمد فاتحة كل كلام

BURSEVI:v1p2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2/r2.claim: It is also a key to the Qur'an's treasures: knowledge of its meanings unlocks ambiguous passages and illuminates its verses.
BURSEVI:v1p2/r2.anchor: لأنها مفتاح كنوز لطائف الخطاب بانجلائها ينكشف جميع القرآن لأهل البيان

BURSEVI:v1p2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2/r3.claim: Fatiha is the Mother of the Qur'an because it gathers the Qur'an's purposes: affirming divinity and prophethood, and establishing decree and predestination.
BURSEVI:v1p2/r3.anchor: أربعة : إقرار بالألوهية والنبوة وإثبات القضاء والقدر

BURSEVI:v1p2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2/r4.claim: The opening praise and names of the Merciful indicate God's divinity.
BURSEVI:v1p2/r4.anchor: {الحمد لله رب العالمين * الرحمن الرحيم} يدل على الألوهية

BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r1.claim: It is called the seven oft-repeated because it has seven verses, each can stand for seven Qur'anic portions, and reciting them is said to earn the whole Qur'an's reward or close seven gates of Hell.
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r1.anchor: لأنها سبع آيات أو لأن كل آية منها تقوم مقام سبع من القرآن

BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r2.claim: The name al-mathani is explained by repetition in prayer or each rak'a, intercession in each rak'a, or revelation twice, in Mecca and Medina.
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r2.anchor: فلأنها تثنى في كل صلاة أو في كل ركعة بالنسبة إلى الأخرى

BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r3.claim: Other names include the Prayer, Healing, Cure, Foundation, Sufficient, Complete, Praise, Supplication, Thanks, and Invocation surahs because their meanings occur in it.
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r3.anchor: وسميت بسورة الصلاة وسورة الشفاء والشافية وأساس القرآن والكافية والوافية

BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r4.claim: It is called the Treasure surah because a report says the Opening is a treasure from God's Throne.
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r4.anchor: وسورة الكنز لما يروى أن الله تعالى قال : "فاتحة الكتاب كنز من كنوز عرشي"

BURSEVI:v1p6/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p6/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p6/r2.claim: The five divine attributes unfold a sequence: God creates, nurtures with favors, conceals sin in mercy, forgives repentance, and finally judges.
BURSEVI:v1p6/r2.anchor: خلقتك فأنا إله ثم ربيتك بالنعم فأنا رب ثم عصيت فسترت عليك فأنا رحمن

BURSEVI:v1p9/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p9/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p9/r4.claim: Bursevi relays the Najmiyya interpretation that the self has four faculties, matched by four divine attributes that draw the servant toward God.
BURSEVI:v1p9/r4.anchor: فللنفس أربع صفات : أمارة ، ولوامة ، وملهمة ، ومطمئنة

SULAMI:v1p35#2/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r1.speaker: author
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r1.claim: Al-Rahman oversees the secrets of saints and unveils Himself to prophets' spirits; al-Rahim tenderly sustains all creatures, good and wicked, in worldly life.
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r1.anchor: بالإشراف على أسرار أوليائه والتجلي لأرواح أنبيائه والرحيم بالعطف على أنفس الخلائق

SULAMI:v1p35#2/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r2.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r2.claim: One view makes al-Rahman specific in both name and action, and al-Rahim general in both.
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r2.anchor: وقيل : الرحمن خاص الاسم خاص الفعل والرحيم عام الاسم عام الفعل

SULAMI:v1p35#2/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r3.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r3.claim: Al-Rahman gives blessings, while al-Rahim grants protection from sin.

SULAMI:v1p35#2/r4.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r4.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r4.claim: Al-Rahman signifies divine disclosure, al-Rahim divine governance.

SULAMI:v1p35#2/r5.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r5.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r5.claim: Al-Rahman reveals lights and al-Rahim preserves entrusted secrets.
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r5.anchor: وقيل : الرحمن بكشف الأنوار والرحيم لحفظ ودائع الأسرار

SULAMI:v1p35#2/r6.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r6.speaker: author
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r6.claim: God's names cannot be comprehended in their true reality; they reveal only creatures' share, and whoever claims to explain God's essence through them goes astray, since God is beyond knowledge (20:110).
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r6.anchor: وجل الحق أن يدرك حقيقة أساميه أحد ؛ لأن أسماءه بلا علة

SULAMI:v1p35#2/r7.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r7.speaker: جعفر
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r7.claim: Al-Rahman supplies outward food, drink, and health as well as inward intellect, knowledge, understanding, senses, and aspiration.
SULAMI:v1p35#2/r7.anchor: الرحمن الذي يرزق الخلق ظاهرا وباطنا ، فرزق الظاهر الأقوات من المأكولات

IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r1.claim: In a sacred report, God says that when the worshipper says praise belongs to God, the servant has praised Him, and when he says the two mercy names, he has extolled Him.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r1.anchor: قال رسول لله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - يقول الله : قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي ، فاذا قال الحمد لله رب العالمين ، قال : مدحني عبدي

IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r2.speaker: الضحاك
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r2.claim: Al-Dahhak says al-Rahman encompasses all creation, while al-Rahim is specifically for believers.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r2.anchor: عن الضحاك في قوله : الرحمن الرحيم قال : الرحمن بجميع خلقه ، والرحم بالمؤمنين خاصة

IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r3.speaker: خالد بن صفوان
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r3.claim: Khalid ibn Safwan says both names convey tenderness, with one more tender than the other.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r3.anchor: حدثني خالد بن صفوان التميمي في قوله : الرحمن الرحيم قال : هما رقيقان احدهما ارق من الاخر

IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r4.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r4.claim: Al-Hasan repeats that al-Rahman is a name people cannot appropriate for themselves.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r4.anchor: عن الحسن قال : الرحمن اسم لا يستطيع الناس ان ينتحلوه

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r1.claim: He reads the sura's annexation to Fatihat al-Kitab as descriptive: it means a sura characterized as the Book's opening, with no separate title needed.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r1.anchor: إضافة السورة إلى فاتحة الكتاب من إضافة الموصوف إلى الصفة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r2.claim: By contrast, Fatihat al-Kitab is a true annexation: al-Kitab here means the remainder of the Book apart from the sura called the Opening.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r2.anchor: إضافة فاتحة إلى الكتاب فإضافة حقيقية باعتبار أن المراد من الكتاب بقيته

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r3.claim: The names Umm al-Qur'an and Umm al-Kitab are established in the Sunna; “mother” denotes a thing's origin and source.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r3.anchor: وأما تسميتها أم القرآن وأم الكتاب فقد ثبتت في السنة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r4.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r4.claim: A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says Abu Sa'id al-Khudri recited Umm al-Qur'an over a person suffering from a sting as a healing prayer.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r4.anchor: أن أبا سعيد الخدري رقى ملدوغا فجعل يقرأ عليه بأم القرآن

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r5.speaker: النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r5.claim: A sound hadith calls a prayer without Umm al-Qur'an deficient.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r5.anchor: كل صلاة لم يقرأ فيها بأم القرآن فهي خداج

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r6.claim: One explanation of Umm al-Qur'an is that it begins and opens the Qur'an, making it like its origin.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r6.anchor: أنها مبدؤه ومفتتحه فكأنها أصله ومنشؤه

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r7.claim: A second explanation is that the sura gathers the Qur'an's three main aims: praise, commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r7.anchor: تشتمل محتوياتها على أنواع مقاصد القرآن وهي ثلاثة أنواع

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r8.claim: The opening praise gathers God's praised attributes, declares His uniqueness in divinity, and affirms resurrection and recompense.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r8.anchor: الثناء على الله ثناء جامعا لوصفه بجميع المحامد وتنزيهه عن جميع النقائص

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r11.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r11.claim: The sura's three aims together represent the Qur'an's original purposes, while its remaining material elaborates them.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r11.anchor: فهذه هي أنواع مقاصد القرآن كله ، وغيرها تكملات لها

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r12.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r12.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r12.claim: He also supports the sura's comprehensiveness by citing the sound report that al-Ikhlas counts as a third of the Qur'an because all its wording praises God.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r12.anchor: وقد يؤيد هذا الوجه بما ورد في الصحيح في : { قل هو الله أحد }

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r1.claim: A third explanation of Umm al-Qur'an is that it contains the Qur'an's theoretical wisdom and practical rulings, including theology, prophecy, admonition, worship, transactions, morals, and law.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r1.anchor: تشتمل معانيها على جملة معاني القرآن من الحكم النظرية والأحكام العملية

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r4.claim: The names al-Rahman and al-Rahim encompass the foundations of legislation as mercy toward those charged with duties.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r4.anchor: يشمل أصول التشريع الراجعة للرحمة بالمكلفين

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r11.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r11.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r11.claim: Taken explicitly and by implication, the sura gives a general outline of the Qur'an's aims and prompts readers to seek their fuller detail as able.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r11.anchor: يحصل من معاني الفاتحة تصريحا وتضمنا علم إجمالي بما حواه القرآن

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r12.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r12.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r12.claim: Requiring al-Fatiha in every rak'ah preserves recollection of the Qur'an's purposes contained within it.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r12.anchor: فرضت قراءة الفاتحة في كل ركعة من الصلاة حرصا على التذكر

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r10.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r10.speaker: النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r10.claim: A hadith in both Sahihs from Abu Hurayra has God divide prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each portion of al-Fatiha and granting the servant's request.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r10.anchor: قسمت الصلاة نصفين بيني وبين عبدي فنصفها لي ونصفها لعبدي

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r11.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r11.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r11.claim: The verse division differs by region: Medinans exclude the basmala and count “those You favored” as a verse; Meccans and Kufans include the basmala and combine that phrase with its verse; Hasan counts both separately.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r11.anchor: فعند أهل المدينة لا تعد البسملة آية وتعد : { أنعمت عليهم } آية

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r1.claim: The opening-revelation report supplies another argument: the Prophet recounts the command “Read in the name of your Lord” without the formula “In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate.”
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r1.anchor: فلم يقل فقال لي بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم { اقرأ بسم ربك }

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r2.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r2.claim: Al-Razi answers the objection to repeating al-Rahman al-Rahim by saying repetition for emphasis is common in the Qur'an and stressing God's mercy is important.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r2.anchor: إن التكرار لأجل التأكيد كثير في القرآن

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r3.claim: Ibn Ashur rejects al-Razi's answer: the Fatiha has no suitable rhetorical purpose for such repetition, and its short distance violates eloquent avoidance of needless repetition.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r3.anchor: إلا أن الفاتحة لا مناسبة لها بأغراض التكرير

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r4.speaker: البيضاوي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r4.claim: Al-Baydawi says the repeated attributes explain why God deserves praise.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r4.anchor: بأن نكتة التكرير هنا هي تعليل استحقاق الحمد

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r5.claim: Ibn Ashur says this answer fails: if praise needs both attributes, avoiding repetition would require removing them from the opening basmala, producing an awkward wording.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p141/r5.anchor: فدفع التكرير يقتضي تجريد البسملة التي في أول الفاتحة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p150/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p150/r5.speaker: البيضاوي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p150/r5.claim: Al-Baydawi explains pairing God's proper name with al-Rahman and al-Rahim as invoking His entitlement to assistance and mercy: al-Rahman signals the gifts involved in righteous action, with al-Rahim explained later.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p150/r5.anchor: ثم يذكر وصف الرحمن إشارة إلى أن الاستعانة على الأعمال الصالحة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r1.claim: Important guidance requires preparing listeners, stirring their attention, and removing stubbornness, false assumptions, and satanic impulses that block learning.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r1.anchor: ما بقي يخالجها العناد والبهتان ، وتخامر رشدها نزغات الشيطان

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r10.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r10.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r10.claim: As a Qur'anic preface, al-Fatiha models an Arabic literary opening that improves understanding and attentive reception.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r10.anchor: وهذا الأسلوب له شأن عظيم في صناعة الأدب العربي

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r5.claim: Because the Qur'an guides people and reforms both worldly and future life, listeners must prepare by removing stubbornness, error, and low impulses before receiving its wisdom.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r5.anchor: فلا مناص لها قبل استقبال تلك الحكمة والنظر من الاتسام بميسم الفضيلة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r10.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r10.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r10.claim: These aims help explain why al-Fatiha is called Umm al-Qur'an.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r10.anchor: ولأجل هذا سميت هاته السورة أم القرآن

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r1.speaker: المبرد
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r1.claim: Al-Mubarrad, quoted by Ibn al-Anbari in al-Qurtubi's commentary, says الرحمن is a Hebrew loan whose khāʾ became Arabic حاء, citing Jarir's poem.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r1.anchor: أن الرحمن اسم عبراني نقل إلى العربية

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r2.claim: Ibn Ashur finds no evidence that الرحمن is Hebrew: Arabic and Hebrew are sister languages, Arabic may be older, and the pagans' question in 25:60 need not mean the word was non-Arabic.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r2.anchor: ولم يأت المبرد بحجة على ما زعمه

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r3.claim: Human mercy begins as a tender inward response that moves a person to kindness and aid; when attributed to God it denotes the outward acts of mercy, not a created emotional state, in keeping with transcendence.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p169/r3.anchor: فأصل الرحمة من مقولة الانفعال وآثارها من مقولة الفعل

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r1.speaker: أبو حامد الغزالي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r1.claim: Al-Ghazali says a person who wants to meet a need but cannot do so may be called compassionate for the feeling, but is deficient; the complete quality produces its effect.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r1.anchor: الذي يريد قضاء حاجة المحتاج ولا يقضيها

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r2.claim: Applying الرحمن الرحيم to God is not ambiguous: common usage makes the intended sense clear, while reason excludes creaturely limitations, as with divine knowledge, life, and power.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r2.anchor: ليس من المتشابه لتبادر المعنى المراد منه بكثرة استعماله

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r3.claim: Scripture uses God's mercy for His willing beneficence to creatures in worldly life, as in 7:156; most divine names similarly carry a scriptural sense freed from creaturely limits.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r3.anchor: فهي منقولة في لسان الشرع إلى إرادة الله إيصال الإحسان

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r4.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r4.claim: Al-Kashshaf and many investigators treat الرحمن as an adjective of enduring quality; a transitive verb can shift to an intransitive habitual form before forming this adjective.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r5.speaker: ابن مالك
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r5.claim: Ibn Malik objects to treating الرحمن as an adjective of enduring quality because its source رحم is transitive, and compares it with رب and ملك.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p170/r5.anchor: ومن النحاة من منع أن يكون الرحمن صفة مشبهة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r1.speaker: سيبويه
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r1.claim: Sibawayh treats الرحيم as an intensive form that remains transitive; al-Kashshaf and most scholars instead call it an adjective of enduring quality, though both analyses convey intensity. Ibn Ashur sides with Sibawayh.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r2.claim: Both adjectives intensify mercy, but usage supports the principle that added form usually adds force: al-Zajjaj glosses غضبان as full of anger, and Arabs lengthened الشقدف to الشقنداف for a heavier camel litter; the rule has exceptions.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r3.speaker: الجمهور
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r3.claim: Most authorities, including Abu Ubayda, Ibn Jinni, al-Zajjaj, and al-Zamakhshari, consider الرحمن more intense because its form is longer; interpreters explain the pairing by making it more specific and الرحيم broad in its objects.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r3.anchor: قال الجمهور إن الرحمن أبلغ من الرحيم

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r4.claim: الرحمن is restricted to God, while الرحيم describes mercy reaching many recipients and can also describe the Messenger; therefore the second adjective adds meaning instead of repeating the first.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p171/r4.anchor: ومدلول الرحيم كون الرحمة كثيرة التعلق

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r1.claim: الرحمن precedes الرحيم because a description of God's intrinsic quality should come before a description of how widely its effects reach.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r1.anchor: لأن الصيغة الدالة على الاتصاف الذاتي أولى بالتقديم

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r2.speaker: قطرب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r2.claim: Qutrub treats الرحمن and الرحيم as synonyms and their pairing as emphatic repetition; al-Zajjaj leans toward this view, which Ibn Ashur rejects because emphasis is not warranted here.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r2.anchor: أن الرحمن والرحيم يدلان على معنى واحد

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r3.speaker: جمهور الأئمة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r3.claim: Most leading scholars say الرحمن was not used of God by Arabs before Islam; Quranic challenges and repeated Meccan references suggest the name was unfamiliar or contested, and some take it as God's proper name.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r3.anchor: أن وصف الرحمن لم يطلق في كلام العرب قبل الإسلام

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r4.claim: The Meccan verse about what holds the birds uses الرحمن, while the Medinan portion of al-Nahl uses الله, subtly reinforcing the divine name in its Meccan setting.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r4.anchor: ما يمسكهن إلا الرحمن في سورة الملك

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r5.claim: The poet who called Musaylima رحمانا wrote after Islam during the Yamama revolt; رحمان اليمامة was an extremist title, not evidence of pre-Islamic usage.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r5.anchor: فإنما قاله بعد مجيء الإسلام وفي أيام ردة أهل اليمامة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r6.claim: The sequence suits the context: after describing God as the world's nurturer and completer, it names the mercy creatures need from Him as their weak Lord's dependents.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p172/r6.anchor: وكان المربوبون ضعفاء كان احتياجهم للرحمة واضحا

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p173/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p173/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p173/r1.claim: Although nurture brings creatures toward completion, it can involve hardship; الرحمن assures that God's benefits and laws reach people gently, with ease and without undue burden, including public benefits such as zakat.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p173/r1.anchor: تنبيها على أن تلك النعم الجليلة وصلت إلينا بطريق الرفق واليسر

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p173/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p173/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p173/r2.claim: The grammarians dispute whether an indefinite رحمان takes tanwin; Banu Asad decline all faʿlan forms with a feminine faʿlana, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Radi, and Ibn Malik prefer leaving it uninflected.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p173/r2.anchor: واختار الزمخشري والرضى وابن مالك عدم صرفه

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r8.speaker: أم سلمة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r8.claim: A report from Umm Salama has a pause after Rahim before al-hamdu, with a cut initial alif; some Kufans read this way.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r8.anchor: فروي عن أم سلمة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم الرحيم الحمد تسكن الميم ويوقف عليها

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r9.speaker: جمهور الناس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r9.claim: Most readers connect Rahim grammatically to al-hamdu by genitive inflection and joining the alif of al-hamdu; one may explain the vowel as resolving adjacent consonants.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r9.anchor: وقرأ جمهور الناس الرحيم الحمد يعرب الرحيم بالخفض، وتوصل الألف من الحمد

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r10.speaker: الكسائي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r10.claim: Al-Kisaʾi cites an Arab reading with an opened mim and joined alif, but the author knows of no one who transmitted it as a reading.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p63#2/r10.anchor: وحكى الكسائي عن بعض العرب أنها تقرأ الرحيم الحمد بفتح الميم وصلة الألف

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12#2/r1.speaker: أبو العاليه وابن السميفع وعيسى بن عمر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12#2/r1.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya, Ibn al-Sumayfa, and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read both divine names in the accusative.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12#2/r1.anchor: قرأ أبو العاليه وابن السميفع وعيسى بن عمر بالنصب فيهما

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12#2/r2.speaker: أبو رزين العقيلي والربيع بن خيثم وأبو عمران الجوني
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12#2/r2.claim: Abū Razīn, al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, and Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī read both names in the nominative.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12#2/r2.anchor: وقرأ أبو رزين العقيلي والربيع بن خيثم وأبوا عمران الجوني بالرفع فيهما

IBNKATHIR:1:3/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:3/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:3/r1.claim: Ibn Kathir says his discussion of al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm under the basmala already covers these names, so he does not repeat it here.

IBNKATHIR:1:5/r11.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:5/r11.speaker: الله تعالى
IBNKATHIR:1:5/r11.claim: In a divine report, God divides the prayer between Himself and His servant, responds to each recited section, calls 1:5 shared between them, and grants the servant's request.
IBNKATHIR:1:5/r11.anchor: قال : هذا بيني وبين عبدي ولعبدي ما سأل

JISHUMI:v1p200/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p200/r10.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p200/r10.claim: Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm derive from mercy, whose basis is benefaction to the needy; both are intensive forms, with faʿlān more emphatic than faʿīl because it departs further from the base pattern.
JISHUMI:v1p200/r10.anchor: والرحمن الرحيم: اسمان مشتقان من الرحمة، وأصل الرحمة: النعمة

JISHUMI:v1p203/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r6.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r6.claim: One view treats al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as synonymous names for the merciful, like nadmān and nadīm.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r6.anchor: قيل: معناهما واحد، وهو ذو الرحمة، كندمان ونديم

JISHUMI:v1p203/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r7.claim: Another view distinguishes the names because other beings may be called raḥīm but not raḥmān.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r7.anchor: وقيل: بينهما فرق، ولذلك يسمى غيره رحيما، ولا يسمى رحمانا

JISHUMI:v1p203/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r8.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r8.claim: One distinction makes al-Raḥmān the provider for all creatures and al-Raḥīm the forgiver of all believers.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r8.anchor: قيل: الرحمن: الرازق لجميع خلقه، والرحيم: الغافر لجميع المؤمنين

JISHUMI:v1p203/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r9.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r9.claim: Another makes al-Raḥmān the giver of foundational blessings only God can create, while al-Raḥīm denotes one possessing mercy.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r9.anchor: الرازق لجميع خلقه، والرحيم: الغافر لجميع المؤمنين، وقيل: الرحمن: فاعل أصول النعم

JISHUMI:v1p203/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r10.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r10.claim: A further distinction assigns al-Raḥmān to creation and al-Raḥīm to provision.

JISHUMI:v1p203/r11.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r11.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r11.claim: The pairing intensifies the attribution of mercy and teaches that all blessings come from God.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r11.anchor: للمبالغة بصفته بالرحمة؛ ليعلم أن النعم كلها منه

JISHUMI:v1p203/r12.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r12.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r12.claim: Because Arabs commonly knew Allah but not al-Raḥmān, the names are paired to show that Allah, al-Raḥmān, and al-Raḥīm all name and describe Him.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r12.anchor: لأن العرب كثير في لغتهم لفظ، (الله)، ولم يعرفوا الرحمن، فجمع بينهما

JISHUMI:v1p203/r13.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r13.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r13.claim: Another explanation says al-Raḥmān is more frequent in the Torah, al-Raḥīm in the Gospel, and Allah in the Qur’an, so the pairing shows all refer to God.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r13.anchor: لأن في التوراة ذكر الرحمن أكثر، وفي الإنجيل ذكر الرحيم أكثر، وفي القرآن ذكر الله أكثر

JISHUMI:v1p203/r14.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r14.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r14.claim: Al-Raḥmān precedes al-Raḥīm because its stronger intensity and exclusive use make it like a proper name, and the more definite name comes first.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r14.anchor: لأنه لما كان أشد مبالغة، ولا يوصف به غيره صار كالعلم

JISHUMI:v1p206/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r7.claim: Al-Raḥmān gives the blessings of worldly life and religion; al-Raḥīm has expansive mercy, and the whole praise belongs to the One who creates, owns, blesses, and deserves worship.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r7.anchor: المنعم بنعم الدنيا والدين. الرحيم: واسع الرحمة

JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.claim: Explanations for repeating al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm: the first occurrence is outside the sūra, it first seeks aid and the second assigns praise to God, or the repetition emphasizes mercy.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.anchor: قيل: لأن الأول ليس من السورة

JISHUMI:v1p206/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r9.speaker: علي بن عيسى
JISHUMI:v1p206/r9.claim: ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā denies mere repetition: the first occurrence links servitude to blessings warranting worship, the second links praise to blessings warranting praise.

MAJAZ:v1p21/r1.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p21/r1.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p21/r1.claim: Al-Raḥmān means possessor of mercy, while al-Raḥīm means merciful; Arabic can use two forms from one word with one meaning.
MAJAZ:v1p21/r1.anchor: «الرحمن» مجازه ذو الرحمة، و «الرحيم» مجازه الراحم، وقد يقدرون اللفظين من لفظ واحد والمعنى واحد،

MAJAZ:v1p21/r2.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p21/r2.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p21/r2.claim: This pairing reflects Arabic breadth of expression, like nadmān and nadīm; Burj ibn Mushir’s verse uses nadmān for a drinking companion.
MAJAZ:v1p21/r2.anchor: قال برج بن مسهر الطائى، جاهلى: وندمان يزيد الكأس طيبا ... سقيت وقد تغورت النجوم

MAJAZ:v1p21/r3.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p21/r3.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p21/r3.claim: Al-Nuʿmān ibn Naḍla’s verse likewise uses nadmān for a companion, illustrating the paired forms.
MAJAZ:v1p21/r3.anchor: وقال النعمان بن نضلة، عدوى من عدى قريش: فإن كنت ندمانى فبالأكبر اسقني ... ولا تسقنى بالأصغر المتثلم

MAJAZ:v1p21/r4.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p21/r4.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p21/r4.claim: Barīq al-Hudhalī’s verse calls Abū Zayd both brother and nadīm, witnessing the companion sense of nadīm.
MAJAZ:v1p21/r4.anchor: وقال بريق الهذلى عدوى من عدى قريش: رزينا أبا زيد ولا حى مثله ... وكان أبو زيد أخى ونديمى»

MAJAZ:v1p21/r5.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p21/r5.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p21/r5.claim: Ḥassān ibn Thābit also uses nadīm for a drinking companion in support of the Arabic synonym pair.
MAJAZ:v1p21/r5.anchor: وقال حسان بن ثابت: لا أخدش الخدش ولا ... يخشى نديمى إذا انتشيت يدى

MUQATIL:1:1-4/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:1:1-4/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:1:1-4/r3.claim: Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are two closely related names, one more delicate than the other; al-Raḥmān means merciful and al-Raḥīm means compassionate through mercy.
MUQATIL:1:1-4/r3.anchor: اسمان رفيقان، أحدهما أرق من الآخر

MUQATIL:1:5-7/r8.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:1:5-7/r8.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
MUQATIL:1:5-7/r8.claim: A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet related that God divided this sūra between Himself and the servant: praise is thanks, the two mercy names are praise, the King verse is glorification, and the rest belongs to the servant; seeking help is God's special acknowledgment of the servant's plea.
MUQATIL:1:5-7/r8.anchor: عن أبى هريرة، أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

NASAFI-FULL:v1p7/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p7/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p7/r1.claim: Repeating Rahman and Rahim here supports the conclusion that the basmala is not part of al-Fatiha, since repetition would otherwise add no information.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p7/r1.anchor: ذكرهما قد مر وهو دليل على أن التسمية ليست من الفاتحة إذ لو كانت منها لما أعادهما لخلو الاعادة عن الافادة

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r12.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r12.claim: Qatada says al-ʿālamūn is all that exists apart from God, a collective with no singular of the same form, like raht or qawm.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r12.anchor: فقال قتادة: العالمون جمع عالم، وهو كل موجود سوى الله تعالى

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r13.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r13.claim: Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl says the worlds are the people of each era, as the verse about men approaching men uses the term for people.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r13.anchor: وقيل: أهل كل زمان عالم قاله الحسين بن الفضل لقوله تعالى:

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the worlds are jinn and humans, since the warning to the worlds did not include animals.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r1.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: العالمون الجن والإنس دليله قوله تعالى:

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r2.speaker: الفراء وأبو عبيدة
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r2.claim: Al-Farraʾ and Abu ʿUbayda restrict “worlds” to rational beings—humans, jinn, angels, and devils—because this plural is for rational beings, not animals.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r2.anchor: وقال الفراء وأبو عبيدة: العالم عبارة عمن يعقل وهم أربع أمم: الإنس والجن والملائكة والشياطين.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r3.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r3.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ describe the worlds as provisioned beings or spiritual beings; Ibn ʿAbbas also says every living creature moving on earth.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r3.anchor: وقال زيد بن أسلم: هم المرتزقون ونحوه قول أبي عمرو بن العلاء: هم الروحانيون.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r4.speaker: وهب بن منبه
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r4.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih says God has 18,000 worlds, of which this world is one.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r4.anchor: إن لله عز وجل ثمانية عشر ألف عالم الدنيا عالم منها

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r5.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r5.claim: Abu Saʿid al-Khudri says God has 40,000 worlds, with the world from east to west counted as one.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r5.anchor: إن لله أربعين ألف عالم الدنيا من شرقها إلى غربها عالم واحد

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r6.speaker: مقاتل
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r6.claim: Muqatil says there are 80,000 worlds: 40,000 on land and 40,000 in the sea.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r6.anchor: وقال مقاتل: العالمون ثمانون ألف عالم، أربعون ألف عالم في البر، وأربعون ألف عالم في البحر.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r7.speaker: الربيع بن أنس عن أبي العالية
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r7.claim: Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas transmits from Abu al-ʿAliya that jinn and humans are worlds and each of earth’s four corners has 1,500 worlds created to worship God.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r7.anchor: وروى الربيع بن أنس عن أبي العالية قال: الجن عالم، والإنس عالم وسوى ذلك للأرض أربع زوايا

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r8.claim: The broadest view is soundest: worlds comprise every creature and existent, as Pharaoh’s question and God’s answer define them as the heavens, earth, and all between.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r8.anchor: والقول الأول أصح هذه الأقوال لأنه شامل لكل مخلوق وموجود

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r9.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r9.claim: Al-Zajjaj derives ʿālam from knowledge or a sign: every created thing indicates its Maker; al-Khalil similarly says the world points to a Creator and manager.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r9.anchor: العالم كل ما خلقه الله في الدنيا والآخرة

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r10.claim: The author recounts a man who said alhamdulillah without mentioning the worlds; Junayd told him to complete God’s wording, since a created thing leaves no trace when paired with the Eternal.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r10.anchor: المحدث إذا قرن مع القديم لا يبقى له أثر

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r11.claim: Rabb may be read nominative as an independent clause, “He is Lord of the worlds,” or accusative as praise.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r11.anchor: الثانية عشرة: يجوز الرفع والنصب في «رب» فالنصب على المدح، والرفع على القطع أي هو رب العالمين.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r12.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r12.claim: God pairs the awe-inspiring “Lord of the worlds” with “the Compassionate, the Merciful,” balancing fear with hope to aid obedience; Muslim reports that each extreme of fear or hope would overwhelm believer or disbeliever.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:3/r12.anchor: لأنه لما كان في اتصافه ب { رب العلمين } ترهيب قرنه ب { الرحمن الرحيم }

NAHHAS:v1p171/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p171/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p171/r1.claim: The paired names may be accusative as praise, both nominative with an implied subject, one nominative and one accusative, or the first genitive with the second nominative or accusative.
NAHHAS:v1p171/r1.anchor: على المدح ويجوز رفعهما على إضمار مبتدأ ويجوز رفع أحدهما ونصب الآخر

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r1.claim: Al-Fatiha is Meccan and has seven verses; Muslims recite it at least seventeen times daily, more with voluntary prayers, and may repeat it without limit.

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.speaker: رسول الله [ ص ]
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.claim: The Prophet says prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening of the Book; the report is in both Sahih collections.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.anchor: لا صلاة لمن لم يقرأ بفاتحة الكتاب

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.claim: The short surah gathers core Islamic creed, worldview, feelings, and guidance, explaining its repetition in every rakʿa and why prayer without it is invalid.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.anchor: ما يشير إلى طرف من حكمة اختيارها للتكرار

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r8.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r8.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r8.claim: Rahman and Rahim together encompass every meaning and condition of mercy; God alone bears both, and alone may be called Rahman, though a servant may be called Rahim.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r8.anchor: فمن الجائز أن يوصف عبد من عباده بأنه رحيم

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r9.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r9.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r9.claim: Quṭb leaves aside which mercy-name has broader scope and stresses that together they cover mercy in all its meanings, conditions, and domains.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r9.anchor: إنما نخلص منه إلى استغراق هاتين الصفتين مجتمعتين لكل معاني الرحمة وحالاتها ومجالاتها

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r10.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r10.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r10.claim: Beginning in God's name expresses the first major Islamic worldview principle, God's oneness and proper reverence; comprehensive mercy expresses the second and defines the bond between God and servants.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r10.anchor: وإذا كان البدء باسم الله وما ينطوي عليه من توحيد الله وأدب معه يمثل الكلية الأولى

QUTB-ZILAL:1:3/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:3/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:3/r1.claim: The repeated mercy-names form a separate verse to underscore mercy as the defining feature of comprehensive lordship and the enduring relationship between Creator and creatures.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:3/r1.anchor: هذه الصفة التي تستغرق كل معاني الرحمة وحالاتها ومجالاتها تتكرر هنا

QUTB-ZILAL:1:3/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:3/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:3/r2.claim: God's bond with servants is mercy and care, which elicit praise, reassurance, and affection, unlike vindictive or capricious gods in Greek myths and the Babel story in Genesis 11.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:3/r2.anchor: إن الرب الإله في الإسلام لا يطارد عباده مطاردة الخصوم والأعداء كآلهة الأولمب في نزواتها وثوراتها كما تصورها أساطير الإغريق

QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2.speaker: رسول الله
QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2.claim: Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who receives what he asks.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2.anchor: عن أبي هريرة عن رسول الله [ ص ] :  "  يقول الله تعالى : قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين

RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r1.claim: Qadir names God's power, illustrated by His ability to send punishment from above or below and to resurrect the dead and reconstruct their fingertips.
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r1.anchor: الأول القادر قال تعالى : ﴿ قل هو القادر على أن يبعث عليكم عذابا من فوقكم

RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r2.claim: Qadeer intensifies the description of God as powerful.
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r2.anchor: هذا اللفظ يفيد المبالغة في وصفه بكونه قادرا

RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r3.claim: Muqtadir is another name for power, used of God in the Quran.
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r3.anchor: الثالث : المقتدر قال تعالى : ^ { وكان الله على كل شيء مقتدرا

RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r4.claim: God uses a plural form of the power name for Himself: We decreed, and how excellent are the decreers.
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r4.anchor: الرابع : عبر عن ذاته بصيغة الجمع في هذه الصفة قال تعالى :

RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r5.claim: King and owner imply power in a particular sense; malik occurs more often than malik meaning owner because kingship is a higher rank.
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r5.anchor: اعلم أن لفظ الملك يفيد القدرة أيضا بشرط خاص ثم إن هذا اللفظ جاء في القرآن على وجوه مختلفة

RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r6.claim: Other power-related forms include Owner of Sovereignty, Sovereign, and the kingdom that belongs to the Merciful on that day and of the heavens and earth.
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r6.anchor: الثالث : مالك الملك قال تعالى : ﴿ قل اللهم مالك الملك ﴾

RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r7.claim: Quwwa is close in meaning to power; Quranic forms include the Strong and Possessor of Strength, the Firm.
RAZI-FULL:v1p118/r7.anchor: لفظ القوة يقرب من لفظ القدرة وقد جاء هذا اللفظ في القرآن على وجوه مختلفة

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r1.claim: Many names indicate the honor of the named; Fātiḥat al-Kitāb is so called because it opens codices, teaching, recitation, and prayer, or because praise opens speech, or because it was the first sura sent down.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r1.anchor: اعلم أن هذه السورة لها أسماء كثيرة وكثرة الأسماء تدل على شرف المسمى

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r2.claim: It is called Sūrat al-Ḥamd because its opening word is praise.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r2.anchor: والثاني : سورة الحمد والسبب فيه أن أولها لفظ الحمد

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r3.claim: It is called the Mother of the Qur’an because its verses encompass the Qur’an’s four central aims: theology, resurrection, prophethood, and divine decree.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r3.anchor: أن أم الشيء أصله والمقصود من كل القرآن تقرير أمور أربعة

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r4.claim: A second reason for calling it the Mother of the Book is that all revelation comprises praise, worshipful service, and requests for unveiling; the sura includes each in that order.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r4.anchor: أن حاصل جميع الكتب الإلهية يرجع إلى أمور ثلاثة

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r5.claim: A third reason is that all knowledge concerns either divine lordship or human servitude: the opening praises God’s mastery, while the remainder shows the servant’s dependence on His aid and guidance.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r5.anchor: معرفة عزة الربوبية أو معرفة ذلة العبودية

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r6.claim: A fourth reason is that the sura gathers theology, religious duties, and spiritual purification: praise and lordship establish divine existence and attributes, worship presents duties, and guidance seeks unveiling.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r6.anchor: أن العلوم البشرية إما علم ذات الله وصفاته وأفعاله وهو علم الأصول وإما علم أحكام الله تعالى وتكاليفه وهو علم الفروع

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r7.claim: In the mystical reading, guidance brings light to the heart, the blessed become polished mirrors reflecting sanctity, and the final plea seeks protection from desire and doubt.

RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r2.claim: In prosperity, God's creation supplies safety and honor; in affliction, He either vindicates victims on Judgment Day or rewards what He sent, so He merits limitless praise.
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r2.anchor: فإن كانت من العباد فالله سبحانه وتعالى وعد بأنه ينتصف للمظلومين في يوم الدين

RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r3.claim: The sequence Lord of the worlds, Merciful, Compassionate, Master of Judgment is, in Razi's view, a rationally unsurpassable ordering of God's attributes.
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r3.anchor: مرتب ترتيبا لا يمكن في العقل وجود كلام أكمل وأفضل منه

RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r1.claim: Although the world contains evil, good predominates: health over illness, satiety over hunger, and ease and joy over painful states.
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r1.anchor: الشر وإن كان كثيرا إلا أن الخير أكثر والمرض وإن كان كثيرا إلا أن الصحة أكثر منه

RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r3.claim: Since beneficial ease and safety predominate, the agent is merciful and beneficent and deserves praise; these familiar facts make the reason for praising God apparent to every rational person.
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r3.anchor: ومن كان غالب أفعاله راحة وخيرا وكرامة وسلامة كان رحيما محسنا

RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r3.claim: God's mercy calms the weak servant's awe: worldly life brings continuing mercies, while after death good is repaid without limit and sin may meet pardon and forgiveness.
RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r3.anchor: فأنا الرحمن الرحيم وأنا مالك يوم الدين فما دمت في هذه الحياة الدنيا لا أخليك عن أقسام رحمتي

RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r4.claim: The cosmos is ordered with optimal perfection, and even atoms testify to God's mercy, favor, and beneficence, leading the servant to call Him Merciful and Compassionate.
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r4.anchor: منظومة على الوصف الأتقن والترتيب الأقوم والكمال الأعلى والمنهج الأسنى

RAZI-FULL:v1p161/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p161/r2.speaker: أم سلمة عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p161/r2.claim: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha while counting the basmala as its first verse, followed by the rest of its verses.
RAZI-FULL:v1p161/r2.anchor: روى الشافعي رضي الله عنه عن مسلم عن ابن جريج عن ابن أبي مليكة عن أم سلمة أنها قالت

RAZI-FULL:v1p162/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p162/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p162/r2.claim: In the divided-prayer report, God calls the basmala glorification, al-Hamd praise, the two mercy names extolling, the Master of Judgment entrustment, and the remaining response a sharing and a request granted.
RAZI-FULL:v1p162/r2.anchor: فإذا قال العبد بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم قال الله سبحانه مجدني عبدي وإذا قال الحمد لله رب العالمين

SAMIN-DURR:1:3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:3/r1.claim: Al-Rahman and al-Rahim may be adjectives or appositives and are also read with accusative or nominative detachment, parsed as for rabb al-alamin; their derivation was already explained in the basmala.
SAMIN-DURR:1:3/r1.anchor: نعت أو بدل، وقرئا منصوبين مرفوعين، وتوجيه ذلك ما ذكر في { رب العالمين

RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r1.claim: Al-Raḥmān gives blessings of a kind servants cannot produce, whereas al-Raḥīm gives blessings of a kind they can produce.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r1.anchor: هو المنعم بما لا يتصور صدور جنسه من العباد

RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r2.speaker: إبراهيم بن أدهم
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r2.claim: Ibrāhīm ibn Adham recounts a raven stealing a loaf and carrying it to a bound man, illustrating providential care.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r2.anchor: حكي عن إبراهيم بن أدهم أنه قال كنت ضيفا لبعض القوم

RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r3.speaker: ذو النون
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r3.claim: Dhū al-Nūn recounts a scorpion riding a frog across the Nile, then killing a snake that threatened a sleeping youth, illustrating unseen protection.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r3.anchor: وروي عن ذي النون أنه قال : كنت في البيت إذ وقعت ولولة

RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r4.claim: A raven chick emerges naked and vulnerable; gnats feed it until it grows feathers and its mother returns, prompting the Arab prayer ‘Provider of the nestling in its nest’ and showing universal mercy.

RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r5.claim: Events may look merciful while harming in reality, like a parent neglecting a child, or appear painful while benefiting, like schooling a child or amputating a diseased hand.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r5.anchor: فالأبله يغتر بالظواهر والعاقل ينظر في السرائر

RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r6.claim: Trials and pain are ultimately wisdom and mercy: abandoning great good to avoid slight evil would be a greater evil, so the wise judge realities rather than appearances.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r6.anchor: إن ترك الخير الكثير لأجل الشر القليل شر كثير

RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r7.claim: Religious duties purify spirits from bodily attachments, while Hell redirects the wicked toward righteous action and toward God.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r7.anchor: المقصود من التكاليف تطهير الأرواح عن العلائق الجسدانية

RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r8.claim: Moses judged by outward appearances and objected to the boat, boy, and wall, while al-Khiḍr acted on hidden realities; disliked events may conceal divine wisdom and mercy.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r8.anchor: فاستنكر تخريق السفينة وقتل الغلام وعمارة الجدار المائل

RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r9.claim: Al-Raḥmān is exclusive to God while al-Raḥīm can describe God or others; the lower name follows because people may hesitate to ask a great Lord for small needs.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189#2/r9.anchor: الرحمن : اسم خاص بالله والرحيم : ينطلق عليه وعلى غيره

RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r1.claim: Adding al-Raḥīm invites requests for even ordinary necessities such as a sandal strap or cooking salt; a report says God told Moses to ask Him for salt and fodder.
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r1.anchor: يا موسى سلني عن ملح قدرك وعلف شاتك

RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r2.claim: Mary was saved from slander by one divine mercy; worshippers recite the two mercy names 34 times daily in prayer, so al-Rāzī hopes for their rescue from punishment.
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r2.anchor: فلما صار ذكر الرحمة مرة واحدة سببا لخلاص مريم

RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r3.claim: God is al-Raḥmān because He creates what humans cannot, transforming impure semen into a beautiful form; He is al-Raḥīm because He returns imperfect obedience as a perfect Garden.
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r3.anchor: أنا رحمن لأنك تسلم إلي نطفة مذرة فأسلمها إليك صورة حسنة

RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r4.claim: A story tells of a dying youth unable to utter the testimony because his mother, whom he had injured, refused to forgive him; when she relents at the threat of burning, his speech returns.
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r4.anchor: اعتقل لسانه عن شهادة أن لا إله إلا الله

RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r5.claim: The mother’s limited mercy would not permit burning her son after carrying and nursing him, so God’s boundless mercy should not burn a believer who professed faith for seventy years.
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r5.anchor: فالرحمن الرحيم الذي لم يتضرر بجنايات عبيده

RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r6.claim: When the Prophet’s tooth was broken, he reportedly prayed for his people’s guidance; his mercy on earth and his concern for his community at resurrection show the effect of being sent as mercy.
RAZI-FULL:v1p190/r6.anchor: اللهم اهد قومي فإنهم لا يعلمون

RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r1.speaker: Prophet
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r1.claim: Reports say the Prophet asked that his community’s accounting be in his own hands, yet he withheld funeral prayer for a debtor of two dirhams and removed ʿĀʾisha over the slander; one mercy cannot repair all creatures.
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r1.anchor: اللهم اجعل حساب أمتي على يدي

RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r2.claim: God tells the Prophet to leave the servants to Him: the Prophet’s single mercy is finite, but God’s mercy is infinite and absorbs every creature’s finite sins.
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r2.anchor: فرحمتي لا نهاية لها ومعصيتهم متناهية

RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r3.speaker: القدرية
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r3.claim: The Qadariyya ask how God can be merciful if He creates people for eternal Hell, creates their disbelief and punishes it, or orders faith then blocks it.
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r3.anchor: كيف يكون رحمانا رحيما من خلق الخلق للنار

RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r4.speaker: الجبرية
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r4.claim: The Jabriyya argue that faith is the greatest mercy; if humans produced it, they rather than God would deserve the names al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm.
RAZI-FULL:v1p191/r4.anchor: أعظم أنواع النعمة والرحمة هو الإيمان

RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.claim: The seven Fatiha verses remove seven vices: praise dispels desire, Lord of the worlds greed, Judgment Day anger, worship and aid pride and vanity, guidance caprice, the favored path unbelief and doubt, and the final phrase innovation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.anchor: فثبت أن هذه الآيات السبع دافعة لتلك الأخلاق القبيحة السبعة

RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r6.claim: “The All-Merciful, the Merciful” describes the one God as completely merciful and generous before, during, and after death.
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r6.anchor: موصوف بكمال الرحمة والكرم والفضل والإحسان قبل الموت وعند الموت وبعد الموت

RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.speaker: الله تعالى
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.claim: In a divine report transmitted by the Prophet, God responds to each Fatiha phrase: the opening remembers Him, praise praises Him, the mercy names magnify Him, Judgment Day glorifies Him or is entrusted to Him, worship belongs to Him, aid relies on Him, and guidance is the servant's request.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.anchor: فإذا قال العبد : بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم يقول الله تعالى ذكرني عبدي

RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.claim: Calling the Fatiha “prayer” shows that religious law serves human interests: people most need knowledge of God's lordship and servitude, which the surah's two halves provide to fulfill the covenant.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.anchor: مدار الشرائع على رعاية مصالح الخلق

RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.claim: Since God names the Fatiha “prayer,” prayer without its recitation does not occur; Razi takes this to establish that reciting it is a pillar, as his school holds.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.anchor: أن عند عدم قراءة الفاتحة وجب أن لا تحصل الصلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r1.claim: Razi supports obligatory Fatiha recitation because the Prophet consistently recited it and commands require following him.

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.claim: The rightly guided caliphs also consistently recited it, and the Prophet commanded Muslims to follow their sunna.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.anchor: أن الخلفاء الراشدين واظبوا على قراءتها

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.claim: Muslims everywhere recite it in prayer, and the Qur'an commands following the path of believers.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.anchor: أن جميع المسلمين شرقا وغربا لا يصلون إلا بقراءة الفاتحة

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r4.claim: The prophetic statement “no prayer without the Opening of the Book” directly supports the requirement.

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.claim: The command to recite what is easy from the Qur'an is obligatory; because reciting other passages is not, the obligatory recitation must be the Fatiha.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.anchor: وظاهره الوجوب فكانت قراءة ما تيسر من القرآن واجبة

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.claim: Reciting the Fatiha is the safer course, following the prophetic instruction to leave what causes doubt for what does not.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.anchor: أن قراءة الفاتحة أحوط فوجب المصير إليها

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.claim: The Prophet's constant practice makes abandoning his command forbidden, and Muslims agree that the Fatiha is better and more complete than another recitation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.anchor: وسابعها : أن الرسول عليه السلام واظب على قراءتها فوجب أن يكون العدول عنه محرما

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.claim: If the superior prayer with the Fatiha discharges the obligation, it does not follow that the inferior prayer with another passage does; the obligation remains due.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.anchor: ولا يلزم من الخروج عن العهدة بالعمل الكامل الخروج عن العهدة بالعمل الناقص

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.claim: Prayer seeks remembrance of the heart, and this concise surah gathers lordship and servitude and is equated with the mighty Qur'an; nothing else can replace it.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.anchor: المقصود من الصلاة حصول ذكر القلب

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.claim: The transmitted report itself says that prayer is not established without the Fatiha.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.anchor: أن هذا الخبر الذي رويناه يدل على أن عند فقدان الفاتحة لا تحصل الصلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p218#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p218#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p218#2/r1.claim: The report that “the All-Merciful, the Merciful” magnifies God differs from the opening formula because praise and Lord of the worlds first establish God's perfection, uniqueness, and beneficence; the mercy names then describe the highest conceivable perfection.
RAZI-FULL:v1p218#2/r1.anchor: فلما قال بعده الرحمن الرحيم دل ذلك على أن الإله الكامل في ذاته المكمل لغيره

RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.claim: The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.
RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.anchor: أن آيات الفاتحة سبع والأعمال المحسوسة أيضا في الصلاة سبعة

RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r3.claim: The mercy names correspond to rising from bowing, as God's mercy raises the servant after humility; the Prophet says God looks mercifully when the servant praises Him while rising.
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r3.anchor: العبد لما تضرع إلى الله في الركوع فيليق برحمته أن يرده

RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.claim: The seven Fatiha verses are the soul of the seven prayer acts, themselves the soul of seven stages of human formation; God is the soul of souls and light of lights.
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.anchor: روح الأرواح ونور الأنوار هو الله تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.claim: Muhammad's ascent has a bodily journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and then the high kingdom, and a spiritual journey from the visible to the unseen and from the unseen to the unseen of the unseen.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.anchor: أما ما يتعلق بعالم الأرواح فله معراجان

RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.claim: The spiritual ascent rises through human spirits, the spirits of the heavens, angels, throne-bearers, and pure spirits detached from bodies, whose worship and love of God exceed human comprehension.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.anchor: ثم تترقى فتنتهي إلى الأرواح المقدسة عن التعلقات بالأجسام

RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.claim: The ascent continues through ever-higher spiritual ranks until God, the source of all good and mercy; thus the spirit-world is the unseen and God's presence the unseen of the unseen.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.anchor: فثبت أن عالم الأرواح هو عالم الغيب وحضرة جلال الربوبية هي غيب الغيب

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.speaker: النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.claim: A prophetic report says God has seventy veils of light; if unveiled, the splendor of His face would burn everything perceived by sight, and only prophetic light reveals the number.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.anchor: إن لله سبعين حجابا من النور لو كشفها لأحرقت سبحات وجهه كل ما أدرك البصر

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.claim: Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.anchor: إن تحفة أمتك الصلاة وذلك لأنها جامعة بين المعراج الجسماني وبين المعراج الروحاني

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.claim: Before beginning the ascent, the worshipper purifies body and clothing for the holy presence and chooses which of opposing companions—angel or devil, reason or desire, truth or falsehood, and so forth—to follow, since settled companionship is hard to break.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.anchor: فإنه إذا استحكمت المرافقة تعذرت المفارقة

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.claim: Raising the hands signals leaving both worlds and directing all inner faculties toward God; “God is greatest” means He exceeds all beings, knowledge, comparison, and even the claim that He is simply greater.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.anchor: فاقطع نظرك عنهما بالكلية ووجه قلبك وروحك وسرك وعقلك وفهمك

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.claim: The opening glorification reveals the lights of divine majesty and moves from declaring God's transcendence to praising Him.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.anchor: ثم قل : سبحانك اللهم وبحمدك وفي هذا المقام تجلى لك نور سبحات الجلال

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.claim: “Blessed is Your name” unveils pre-eternity and eternity, since blessing here indicates abiding beyond extinction and nonexistence.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.anchor: لأن قوله تبارك إشارة إلى الدوام المنزه عن الإفناء والإعدام

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.claim: “Exalted is Your majesty” signifies that God's knowledge and greatness exceed every stated measure.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.anchor: أعلم وأعظم من أن تكون صفات جلاله ونعوت كماله محصورة في القدر المذكور

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.claim: “There is no god but You” means every attribute of majesty and perfection belongs only to God; ultimately reason, speech, understanding, and imagination fail before Him.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.anchor: كل صفات الجلال وسمات الكمال له لا لغيره

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.claim: Most scholars place al-Fātiḥah among the earliest sūrahs revealed in Makkah.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.anchor: to have been revealed in Makkah

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.speaker: Mujāhid
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.claim: Mujāhid says al-Fātiḥah was revealed in Madinah.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.anchor: According to Mujāhid (d. 104/722–23), one of the leading scholars among the second generation of Muslims, this sūrah was revealed in Madinah

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.claim: Most scholars reject a Medinan origin because Muslims needed the sūrah to perform obligatory prayers.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.anchor: Most scholars claim that this is impossible, however, as the Muslims would not have been able to perform their required prayers without it

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.claim: Al-Fātiḥah means The Opening: it opens the Book, each prayer cycle, many everyday acts, and may open the breast to faith.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.anchor: The primary meaning of al-Fātiḥah is “The Opening,” which indicates the sūrah’s function as “the opening of the Book”

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.claim: The sūrah is seen as a synthesis and the Quran’s most important chapter, hence Umm al-kitāb; the title also refers to 3:7 and the celestial archetype of scripture.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.anchor: has been given the title Umm al-kitāb, “Mother of the Book,” a

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.claim: It is called the Mother of the Quran because it contains the meaning of the entire Quran.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.anchor: It is also known as “The Mother of the Quran” (IK, Ṭ), a reference to its containing the meaning of the entire Quran

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r7.claim: Another title, The Seven Oft-Repeated, is linked to 15:87.

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.claim: The title The Cure reflects its reputed healing power for body and soul.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.anchor: is said to have healing powers for both body and soul

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.claim: The title The Foundation reflects the Fātiḥah’s role as a foundation for the whole Quran.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.anchor: because it serves as a foundation

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.claim: As Sūrat al-Ḥamd and Sūrat al-Ṣalāh, the Fātiḥah begins each prayer cycle for Sunnis and many Shiites.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.anchor: the Fātiḥah is recited at the beginning of each

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.claim: Shiite law permits reciting the Fātiḥah in the third and fourth cycles or an alternative formula praising God.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.anchor: In Shiite law one is allowed to recite the Fātiḥah

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.claim: Muslims recite the Fātiḥah at diverse life events; funeral services are called fātiḥah in some lands as an opening from one life to another.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.anchor: It is also recited by Muslims on occasions as diverse as a funeral, a wedding, the birth of a child, the inauguration of an official event

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.claim: The Prophet identifies the Fātiḥah as the greatest sūrah, calling it Praise be to God and the seven oft-repeated, and linking it to 15:87.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.anchor: the Prophet told a man that he would teach him the greatest sūrah; when asked what it was, the Prophet responded

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.speaker: God
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.claim: In a hadith qudsī, God responds to the servant’s praise, magnification, and glorification during the prayer, which is divided between them.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.anchor: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.claim: The Fātiḥah is a prayer encapsulating metaphysical and eschatological realities and teaches the proper human disposition toward God.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.anchor: the Fātiḥah is more than the confessional prayer of Muslims. It is a prayer that encapsulates all the metaphysical and eschatological realities

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.claim: Its structure moves from God’s nature in the first three verses, through the God-human relationship, to human states in the final three.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.anchor: The Fātiḥah thus has a threefold structure: the first three verses deal with the nature of God, the middle verse deals with the relationship between God and human beings

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.claim: A report says nothing like the Fātiḥah was revealed in the Torah, Psalms, Gospel, or Quran.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.anchor: In one the Prophet says, “By Him in Whose Hand lies my soul, in neither the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, nor the Quran was the like of it revealed”

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.speaker: Mujāhid
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.claim: One attribution says Satan was frightened when the Fātiḥah was revealed, among four events; others attribute the saying to the Prophet.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.anchor: attributed by some to Mujāhid (Q) and by

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.claim: The Fātiḥah’s exalted status generated many independent commentaries, often showing how the Quran as a whole is contained in it.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.anchor: The exalted status of the Fātiḥah has resulted in numerous independent commentaries upon it, some numbering hundreds of pages

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.claim: A saying attributed to ʿAlī compresses the Quran into the Fātiḥah, the basmalah, its opening bāʾ, and the diacritical point beneath it.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.anchor: a famous saying attributed to ʿAlī ibn AbīṬālib

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.claim: The point beneath bāʾ can symbolize the Divine Pen’s first drop of ink, which inscribed all archetypes on the Preserved Tablet before creation; thus basmalah marks both Quranic and cosmic beginnings.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.anchor:
This point can be understood to represent the first
drop of ink

STUDYQURAN:1:3/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r1.claim: Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm repeat the basmalah’s names in every sūrah except al-Tawbah, and intensify the meaning of mercy.
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r1.anchor: Both Names are intensifications of the word raḥmah

STUDYQURAN:1:3/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r2.claim: Al-Raḥmān is considered more emphatic and encompassing than al-Raḥīm; it uniquely names God’s mercy that brings existence, while al-Raḥīm concerns sustaining nourishment and can describe creatures, including the Prophet.
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r2.anchor: Al-Raḥmān, which is also the title of Sūrah 55, is considered to be more emphatic, embracing, and encompassing than al-Raḥīm

STUDYQURAN:1:3/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r3.claim: Their relation can be pictured as sunlight over the whole sky and a ray touching an individual creature; 17:110 associates the Compassionate with God’s beautiful Names.
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r3.anchor: al-Raḥmān is like the light of the sun that illuminates the whole sky, and al-Raḥīm is like the particular ray of sunlight that touches a creature

STUDYQURAN:1:3/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r4.claim: In Islamic metaphysics, God’s Breath of the Compassionate upon immutable archetypes brings the world into being, so the world’s existence is the breath of divine compassion.
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r4.anchor: the very existence of the world is in essence nothing but the breath

STUDYQURAN:1:3/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r5.claim: The two Names express universal essential mercy that brings creation forth and particular attributive mercy bestowed on chosen beings, including believers (33:43).
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r5.anchor: Together these two Names refer to two aspects of the Divine Mercy

STUDYQURAN:1:3/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r6.claim: Universal mercy is associated with the Compassionate enthroned (20:5; 25:59); particular mercy sustains each creature differently.
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r6.anchor: The essential and universal Mercy is that of the Compassionate, which God bestows upon all things through their very existence

STUDYQURAN:1:3/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:3/r7.speaker: author
